title: Biodiversity offsetting

definition.text: A system, used mainly by planning authorities and developers, for fully compensating the harm a development does to biodiversity.

facts.text: Offsets are measurable conservation gains designed to make up for significant harm left over after prevention and mitigation; the aim is no net loss of biodiversity, ideally a net gain.
Offsetting is the last step of the mitigation hierarchy: harm must first be avoided, minimised and reversed before what remains is offset.
Practitioners measure the amount, type and quality of habitat a project will damage, then find receptor sites where the same can be re-created.
Offsets must show additionality: a gain in biodiversity that would not have happened anyway.
As of 2019, over 100 countries had or were developing offset policies and more than 37 required offsets by law.
England's Biodiversity Net Gain rule, in force from February 2024, requires developers to show a 10% net gain in biodiversity to get planning permission.
Evidence is mixed: offsets work better in simpler, fast-recovering habitats such as wetlands, and a review found about one-third of policies and offsets reported achieving no net loss.
Critics call offsetting a "licence to trash" that legitimises habitat destruction, and question whether biodiversity in one place can be swapped for biodiversity elsewhere.

contested_note: Supporters and opponents disagree on whether offsets are feasible or ethical, given the difficulty of measuring biodiversity and swapping it between places.

title: Biodiversity banking

definition.text: A market-based form of biodiversity offsetting in which conservation gains are turned into credits that developers can buy to offset their damage.

facts.text: It is also called habitat banking, conservation banking, mitigation banking or biodiversity trading, depending on what is being conserved and where.
At a bank site, work such as reintroducing native plants, removing invasive species or filling ditches to restore a swamp generates credits for gains that would not otherwise happen.
It turns offsets into tradeable assets by creating credits in advance of a development and away from its site.
It grew out of US wetland mitigation banking in the 1980s, which arose from the no net loss policies of the 1970s Clean Water Act.
A bank's land is usually locked in by a conservation easement or covenant that binds future owners, often with a trust fund for long-term management.
More than 100 countries require biodiversity offsetting, but banking frameworks are less widespread.
A 2006 analysis of Canadian habitat banking found 25% of projects achieved no net loss of habitat productivity and 12% a net gain.

notes: Challenges section: deep uncertainties in measurement and credit issuance and risks of commodifying nature (c943d1614287).

definition.text: A biodiversity offset that prevents ecological damage that would almost certainly have happened, rather than restoring or creating habitat.

facts.text: Examples include creating protected areas, removing invasive species, or offering alternative livelihoods to stop deforestation.
Activities without a measurable gain for biodiversity, such as funding general research, do not count as offsets.
Poorly designed offset policies can create perverse incentives that encourage further biodiversity decline.

definition.text: Land offered by a company or individual for payment in return for creating or restoring wildlife habitat to offset damage elsewhere.

facts.text: The habitat work is paid for by developers seeking to offset their impact.
The biodiversity gained at the receptor site should equal or exceed the loss at the original impact site.

definition.text: A unit representing the cost of re-creating a piece of damaged habitat, which developers can buy to offset their impact on biodiversity.

facts.text: Receptor-site land is also valued in credits, covering both the cost of restoring habitat and its long-term management.
This lets developers buy and landowners sell credits, creating a market for keeping and restoring habitat.
